extracted.intended_audience: public commenters, policy advocates, and administrative law practitioners involved in federal rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for crafting and timing public comments in administrative rulemaking, emphasizing early engagement (pre‑NPRM), preserving issues for judicial review, and identifying informal decisionmakers who shape agency outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage pre-proposal when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the comment engage with the agency at the earliest possible stage (ANPRM, petition, pre-proposal meeting)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective comment strategy includes submitting comments to the Advance Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (ANPRM) when issued; petitioning for rulemaking before the agency drafts a proposal; participating in stakeholder meetings, technical workshops, and Reg.gov pre-proposal dockets; and filing FOIA requests on agency working drafts. West's central finding: by the time a rule is published, agency thinking is largely locked in, so pre-proposal participation often matters more than comments on the proposed rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use notice-and-comment to preserve issues for litigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the comment preserve specific issues for judicial review by clearly stating the objection and the requested alternative?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when comments are unlikely to change agency decisions, they serve the substantive function of preserving issues for judicial review and forcing the agency to respond on the record. To preserve an issue, clearly state the legal or factual objection and specify the alternative relief or regulatory language requested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify other decision-makers whose involvement is implicated
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the comment identify other decision-makers (OMB/OIRA, the White House, Congress) whose involvement is implicated?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Informal processes often involve actors outside the issuing agency — notably OMB/OIRA, the White House, congressional committees, and other agencies. Effective strategy may require supplementing public comments with direct engagement of these actors (e.g., targeted outreach, congressional briefings, or coordination with interagency offices).

rubrics_metrics.name: Address informal commitments the agency has already made
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the comment address informal commitments the agency has already made (e.g., as revealed in speeches, draft documents, or guidance)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency thinking may be shaped by prior informal commitments visible in speeches, draft documents, internal guidance, or stakeholder negotiations; comments should recognize and directly address such commitments because they constrain what is still changeable in the rulemaking process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize the stage of the rulemaking and tailor the ask
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the comment recognize the stage of the rulemaking and tailor the ask to what is still movable at that stage?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor the content and requested relief to the procedural stage (pre‑proposal, ANPRM, NPRM, final rule). West emphasizes that proposed-rule comments rarely shift entrenched agency commitments, so requests should be calibrated to what the agency can realistically reconsider given its prior informal processes and commitments.
